title: Mapping-simplex presentations and their marked equivalence criterion
statement:
Use simplicial sets of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones] and categorical equivalences of [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure], and marked objects, Cartesian fibrations and the model $\mathsf M_S$ of [lem-coef-marked-relative-cartesian-model]. Let $n\geq0$ and let $A_0\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow A_n$ be a chain of small simplicial sets. Its marked mapping simplex $M^m(A)	o\Delta^n$ has $r$-simplices $(\alpha,a)$, where $\alpha:[r]	o[n]$ is monotone and $a\in(A_{\alpha(r)})_r$. For $	heta:[s]	o[r]$, first apply $	heta^*$ to $a$, then apply the chain transition $A_{\alpha(r)}	o A_{\alpha	heta(s)}$; this gives the operator on the second coordinate. An edge $(\alpha,a)$ is marked exactly when $a$ is degenerate in $A_{\alpha(1)}$. Its vertex fiber at $i$ is $A_i^ lat$.
Every small Cartesian fibration $Y	o\Delta^n$ admits such a chain and a marked map $q:M^m(A)	o Y^
atural$ whose maps $A_i	o Y_i$ on all vertex fibers are categorical equivalences. Every marked map $q$ with this fiberwise property is a Cartesian equivalence in $\mathsf M_{\Delta^n}$. Equivalently the fiberwise hypothesis can be expressed by requiring $A_i^ lat	o Y_i^
atural$ to be a weak equivalence in the absolute marked model of [lem-coef-marked-point-cartesian-model], where $Y_i^
atural$ marks the equivalences of the quasicategory $Y_i$. The assertions include $n=0$ and empty fibers, and do not assert that $M^m(A)$ is fibrant.

source.place: Section 3.2.2, definition of M, Notation 3.2.2.3, Definition 3.2.2.6 and Proposition 3.2.2.7(1); Proposition 3.2.2.14 for marked equivalence. The equivalent point-model formulation is the mapping test against quasicategories. Read online on 2026-10-17; not archived under literature/. No Stacks tag states this marked simplicial or infinity-categorical result.

proof.text:
First check the prescribed construction. For $\theta:[s]\to[r]$ and $\eta:[t]\to[s]$, the second coordinate of the successive operators is $t_{\alpha\theta(s),\alpha\theta\eta(t)}\eta^*t_{\alpha(r),\alpha\theta(s)}\theta^*a=t_{\alpha(r),\alpha\theta\eta(t)}(\theta\eta)^*a$: transition maps are simplicial and chain composites compose. Identity operators are identities. A degenerate edge has constant $\alpha$ and a degenerate second coordinate, so it is marked. Constant $\alpha=i$ gives exactly $A_i^\flat$. For $n>0$, put $T=\Delta^{\{0,\ldots,n-1\}}$ and $A_{<n}=(A_0\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow A_{n-1})$. Sorting simplices by whether their last vertex is $n$ gives the degreewise pushout, also with the specified markings,
$$M^m(A)=M^m(A_{<n})\amalg_{A_n^\flat\times T^\sharp}(A_n^\flat\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp).$$
The map from the overlap to the first term sends $(\alpha,a)$ to $(\alpha,t_{n,\alpha(r)}a)$. This explicit pushout is the gluing used below.

The inclusion $\{n\}^\sharp\to(\Delta^n)^\sharp$ is marked anodyne. Here is the reduction to the endpoint-prism result, rather than an additional existence assumption. For $n>0$ define the monotone homotopy $H:[1]\times[n]\to[n]$ by $H(0,k)=k$, $H(1,k)=n$. Let $\chi(k)=0$ for $k<n$ and $\chi(n)=1$. The maps $k\mapsto(\chi(k),k)$ and $H$ exhibit the arrow $\{n\}^\sharp\to(\Delta^n)^\sharp$ as a retract of $\{1\}^\sharp\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp\to(\Delta^1)^\sharp\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp$. The latter is the pushout product of $P(\varnothing\to\Delta^0)$ with $\varnothing\to(\Delta^n)^\sharp$, and hence is marked anodyne by the endpoint-prism and pushout-product statements. The $n=0$ inclusion is an identity. Thus for any monomorphism $A\hookrightarrow B$, the pushout product
$$(B^\flat\times\{n\}^\sharp)\amalg_{A^\flat\times\{n\}^\sharp}(A^\flat\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp)\longrightarrow B^\flat\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp$$
is marked anodyne. The relative lifting criterion supplies lifts of it into every naturally marked Cartesian fibration over $\Delta^n$.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 3.2.2.11, the marked-anodyne inclusion (Proposition 3.1.2.3)

proof.text:
Prove the stronger relative assertion by induction on $n$: for every small $A$ and marked map $s:A^ lat	imes(\Delta^n)^\sharp	o Y^
atural$ over $\Delta^n$, there are a chain $B_0\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow B_n$, a map $A	o B_n$, and a marked fiberwise categorical-equivalence map $M^m(B)	o Y^
atural$ through which $s$ factors via the canonical $B_n$-cylinder. Factor $s_n:A	o Y_n$ as a monomorphism $g:A\hookrightarrow B_n$ followed by a trivial Kan fibration $h:B_n	o Y_n$. This factorization stays small. Such $h$ is a categorical equivalence: its boundary lifting property extends along boundary-cell presentations to every monomorphism, making it a trivial fibration in the Joyal weak factorization system. Use the lift of Step 2 with $g$, prescribing $s$ on the $A$-cylinder and $h$ on the final fiber. It gives a marked map $s':B_n^ lat	imes(\Delta^n)^\sharp	o Y^
atural$ extending both. For $n=0$, take the one-term chain $B_0$ and map $h$; this proves the induction base, including its required factorization of $s$.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.2.11, final-fiber factorization and prism lift

proof.text: For $n>0$ pull back $Y$ to $T$ and restrict $s'$ to $B_n^\flat\times T^\sharp$. Pullback preserves Cartesian fibrations and their natural markings, so the relative induction hypothesis applies to this restricted map, with parameter $B_n$. It gives a chain $B_0\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow B_{n-1}$, a map $B_n\to B_{n-1}$, and a marked fiberwise categorical-equivalence map on its mapping simplex. Append $B_n$ to the chain. The two maps agree on $B_n^\flat\times T^\sharp$ by the relative induction hypothesis, so the pushout of Step 1 glues them to a marked map $M^m(B)\to Y^\natural$. Its lower vertex maps are equivalences by induction and its final vertex map is $h$. Moreover, the cylinder map with parameter $A$ factors through the $B_n$-cylinder via $g$, and its glued image is $s$ on both pushout pieces. This proves the stronger assertion. Set $A=\varnothing$ to obtain the existence required in the item. Neither a choice of nonempty fibers nor functoriality of the resulting chain is asserted.

Now fix ANY marked $q:M^m(A)\to Y^\natural$ satisfying the stated fiber hypothesis. We prove its underlying map categorical by induction on $n$. The base $n=0$ is the hypothesis $A_0\to Y_0$. For $n>0$, rigidify and write $C=\mathfrak C[M(A)]$, $D=\mathfrak C[Y]$. They decompose into the full subcategories on vertices over $T$ and over $n$, denoted $C_-,C_+$ and $D_-,D_+$. To check fullness directly, recall that rigidification is the colimit of the subset-poset categories of simplices: every contributing composite has nondecreasing base vertices; a composite whose endpoints both lie in $T$ cannot visit $n$, and one whose endpoints both lie over $n$ remains there. Hence $C_-=\mathfrak C[M(A_{<n})]$, $C_+=\mathfrak C[A_n]$, $D_-=\mathfrak C[Y_T]$, $D_+=\mathfrak C[Y_n]$, and the mapping sets from the plus to the minus part are empty. The restriction of $q$ over $T$ satisfies the induction hypothesis. Rigidification equivalence detection therefore makes the restrictions $C_-\to D_-$ and $C_+\to D_+$ Dwyer--Kan equivalences. In particular the total functor is essentially surjective on $\pi_0$, and the only mapping sets still to check go from the minus to the plus part.

We first derive the all-vertex Cartesian recognition criterion from [lem-coef-infinity-cocartesian-mapping-criterion], retaining BOTH directions. For a simplicial set $E$, define $E^{op}$ by precomposing its operators with $\alpha:[a]\to[b]\mapsto\alpha^{op}$, where $\alpha^{op}(i)=b-\alpha(a-i)$. This exchanges $\Lambda_i^m$ with $\Lambda_{m-i}^m$, so an inner fibration $p:E\to B$ of quasicategories becomes an inner fibration $p^{op}$, and an edge $h:y\to z$ is $p$-Cartesian exactly when $h^{op}:z\to y$ is $p^{op}$-cocartesian. To compare the mapping-space conventions, use the natural pinch equivalences $j:M\to U$ of [lem-coef-infinity-pinch-comparison]. Reversal of the arrow and parameter factors identifies $U_{E^{op}}(a,b)$ with $U_E(b,a)^{op}$; realization of the opposite is identified with realization by reversing barycentric coordinates on each simplex. Reversing $\Delta^2$ exchanges its $01,12$ restrictions and preserves the long-edge restriction. Hence the triangle formula for composition in [lem-coef-infinity-mapping-composition] changes precomposition by $h^{op}$ into postcomposition by $h$. Apply the cited cocartesian iff criterion to $p^{op},h^{op}$ and EVERY vertex $w$. After these natural identifications it says precisely that $h$ is $p$-Cartesian if and only if, for every $w\in E$, the square of spaces
$$\begin{array}{ccc}\operatorname{Map}_E(w,y)&\xrightarrow{h\circ-}&\operatorname{Map}_E(w,z)\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow\\
\operatorname{Map}_B(pw,py)&\xrightarrow{p(h)\circ-}&\operatorname{Map}_B(pw,pz)\end{array}$$
is a homotopy pullback. The square includes the homotopy specified by the triangle-composition construction; all reversal and pinch comparisons commute with $p$. In particular there is no restriction $p(w)=p(y)$. The homotopy-pullback meaning is the path-space one in the cited criterion.

source.place: HTT Proposition 2.4.4.3, obtained by dualizing the existing cocartesian criterion; pinch and triangle conventions as in the cited nodes

proof.text: Use [lem-coef-rigidification-postcomposition-comparison] with $S=Y$: whenever postcomposition by $h$ is a weak equivalence on quasicategorical mapping spaces, strict postcomposition by $[h]$ is one on $\mathfrak C[Y]$. Its component-category identification also gives $\pi_0\mathfrak C[Y_j]\cong hY_j$, preserving objects and edge classes. This supplies both comparisons needed below without assuming rigidification locally Kan.

Continue the induction of Step 5. For $x$ over $k<n$ and $y\in A_n$, let $e:y'\to y$ be the marked edge over $n-1\to n$ of [lem-coef-mapping-simplex-final-edge]. Compare the strictly commutative square of enriched mapping sets with rows
$$C_-(x,y')\xrightarrow{[e]\circ-}C(x,y),\qquad D_-(qx,qy')\xrightarrow{[q(e)]\circ-}D(qx,qy).$$
The upper row is a weak homotopy equivalence by that lemma, and the left column is one by Step 5. The total space $Y$ is a quasicategory by relative marked calculus. Since $q$ is marked, $q(e)$ is Cartesian. Apply Step 6's all-vertex criterion with $w=qx$, whose base is the arbitrary vertex $k<n$. The bottom mapping spaces in its square are $\operatorname{Map}_{\Delta^n}(k,n-1)$ and $\operatorname{Map}_{\Delta^n}(k,n)$; both are points, including when $k<n-1$. Its top postcomposition map is therefore a weak equivalence. Step 7 transfers this particular postcomposition map to composition with $[q(e)]$ in $D=\mathfrak C[Y]$. The fullness checked in Step 5 identifies the displayed source with $D(qx,qy')$. Thus the lower row above is a weak equivalence. Two-out-of-three proves the right column a weak equivalence. The diagonal mapping sets and essential surjectivity were checked in Step 5, so $\mathfrak C[q]$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence. Rigidification detection makes $q$ categorical, completing the induction without assuming $M(A)$ a quasicategory.

source.place: HTT Proposition 3.2.2.10, mixed mapping square, using 2.4.4.3 for all vertices and the composition route proved in Steps 6–7

proof.text:
Use [lem-coef-cartesian-marked-lift-generation] for invariance and reflection of Cartesian edges under equivalences in fibers and under coherent equivalence of relative functors. 

Every $y\in Y_j$ is equivalent within $Y_j$ to some $q(a)$, $a\in(A_j)_0$. Indeed rigidification detection makes $\mathfrak C[A_j]\to\mathfrak C[Y_j]$ essentially surjective on $\pi_0$, and Step 7 identifies the latter category with $hY_j$. Given a Cartesian $d:x\to y$ over $i\to j$, let $c=q(t_{j,i}a)$ and choose a fiber equivalence $v:q(a)\simeq y$. The marked edge $e_a:t_{j,i}a\to a$ has Cartesian image, so choose a triangle composite $b= vq(e_a):c\to y$; it is Cartesian by the cited Cartesian-invariance assertion. The cited mapping-fiber lemma is now used ONLY with test vertices in $Y_i$, where its hypothesis is satisfied. Applied to $d$ at $w=c$ it gives $u:c\to x$ in $Y_i$ with $du\simeq b$ over $i\to j$; applied to $b$ at $w=x$ it gives $t:x\to c$ with $bt\simeq d$. Since the postcomposition maps are equivalences, their injectivity on components at $w=x$ and $w=c$ gives $ut\simeq1_x$ and $tu\simeq1_c$, respectively. Hence $u$ is a fiber equivalence. This explicitly supplies an equivalence of arrows $d\simeq vq(e_a)u^{-1}$.

source.place: HTT Proposition 3.2.2.14, marking reflection expanded using 2.4.4.3 and the source-fiber formula 2.4.4.2; closure derived in this step

proof.text: For any simplicial map $f:Y\to Z$ over $\Delta^n$, with $Z$ Cartesian, functors preserve equivalences and inverse-triangle equations. If $fq$ preserves marked edges, $f(q(e_a))$ is Cartesian. The cited conjugation criterion applied in $Z$ to the fiber equivalences $f(u),f(v)$ then recognizes $f(d)$ as Cartesian. The reverse implication holds because $q$ is marked. Thus $f$ preserves all Cartesian edges exactly when $fq$ preserves the marked edges. For a coherent equivalence of functors, its endpoint equivalences and naturality triangles give the same comparison of the image of each edge; the same criterion proves invariance of the preservation condition.

source.place: HTT Proposition 3.2.2.14, marking reflection expanded using 2.4.4.3 and the source-fiber formula 2.4.4.2; closure derived in this step

proof.text:
Let $Z	o\Delta^n$ be a small Cartesian test fibration. Step 8 and [lem-coef-joyal-functor-equivalence-test] give a coherent equivalence $q^*:\operatorname{Fun}(Y,Z)	o\operatorname{Fun}(M(A),Z)$. Select the vertex maps over $\Delta^n$ which preserve the specified marked edges. The relative flat mapping objects are exactly the full subcategories on these vertices: a parameter simplex with these vertices projects every $(x,t)$ to the fixed base vertex of $x$, and a map to $N([n])$ is determined by vertices. These properties are invariant under coherent equivalence. Indeed projected equivalences in $[n]$ are identities; for marking preservation use the preceding marking-reflection argument and the conjugation node. A functor $f:Y	o Z$ is selected if and only if $fq$ is selected. For markings this was just proved. For the base map, every $y\in Y_i$ is fiber equivalent to some $q(a)$; its image has the same base vertex as $fq(a)$, and maps to $N([n])$ with the same vertices agree. Thus [lem-coef-quasicategory-full-subcategory-core-equivalence] applies to these selected full subcategories and gives a weak equivalence on cores. Relative marked calculus identifies those cores with $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_{\Delta^n}(Y^
atural,Z^
atural)$ and $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_{\Delta^n}(M^m(A),Z^
atural)$. The defining Cartesian-equivalence test therefore holds for this arbitrary $Z$.

For $b:B	o E$ with $E$ a quasicategory, maps $E^
atural	o C^
atural$ are all simplicial maps: functors preserve equivalences by the inverse triangles. Maps out of $B^ lat$ impose no condition. Absolute marked mapping calculus identifies the sharp tests with $\operatorname{Fun}(E,C)^\simeq	o\operatorname{Fun}(B,C)^\simeq$. The core-test criterion [lem-coef-marked-flat-categorical-equivalence-test] therefore identifies absolute marked weak equivalence of $B^ lat	o E^
atural$ with categorical equivalence of $b$. Apply this with $B=A_i$, $E=Y_i$. Pullback and induced-marking compatibility of relative marked calculus identify the marking on $Y_i$ with the Cartesian edges of $Y_i	o\Delta^0$. Step 6's IFF criterion for this map says that an edge $h:y	o z$ is Cartesian exactly when $h\circ-:\operatorname{Map}_{Y_i}(w,y)	o\operatorname{Map}_{Y_i}(w,z)$ is an equivalence for every $w$. If $h$ is invertible these maps have inverse postcomposition by $h^{-1}$. Conversely surjectivity on components at $w=z$ gives $g:z	o y$ with $hg\simeq1_z$; injectivity at $w=y$, applied to $hgh\simeq h$, gives $gh\simeq1_y$. The inverse-triangle characterization then makes $h$ an equivalence. Thus the induced marking is exactly the natural equivalence marking, with both implications justified. Thus this is the claimed equivalent fiber hypothesis. The formulas and both inductions included $n=0$; empty fibers impose no nonemptiness requirement in any lifting or equivalence test. In particular $Y_i=\varnothing$ forces $A_i=\varnothing$ whenever a fiber equivalence is given, and if all fibers are empty the sharp mapping complexes out of the empty total space are points, not empty spaces. No part of the argument asserts fibrancy of $M^m(A)$.
